newsitem.title: FRANCE: French polls highlight Chirac's election gamble.
newsitem.headline: French polls highlight Chirac's election gamble.

text.p: At least half French voters believe conservative Jacques Chirac should soldier on as president if the left wins a snap parliamentary election, but a large percentage think he should quit, surveys said on Tuesday.
A CSA opinion poll for the weekly L'Evenement du Jeudi said 55 percent of 812 people questioned wanted Chirac to stay and work with a left-wing prime minister to 33 percent who wanted him to resign.

A BVA poll of 959 people for the weekly Paris Match put the figures at 50 percent and 41 percent respectively, highlighting the gamble Chirac took by calling the May 25-June 1 election in which the left is seen running neck-and-neck with the ruling centre-right.
The CSA poll also said that only 36 percent would vote for Chirac, compared to 49 percent who would not, if a presidential election was held now.
Chirac is to mark on Wednesday the second anniversary of his election for a seven-year term with a bid to rescue the conservatives with an article in provincial newspapers.
The BVA survey, also looking at voters' preferences for the premiership after the parliamentary election, highlighted the unpopularity of Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
Only nine percent wanted Juppe to retain his job if the centre-right retained power.
Twenty-two percent wanted ex-premier Edouard Balladur, Chirac's fellow-Gaullist defeated presidential rival, to return as prime minister.
Eighteen percent preferred former National Assembly speaker and anti-Maastricht campaigner Philippe Seguin, and 13 percent ultra liberal ex-finance minister Alain Madelin.
If the left won, 43 percent of voters wanted former European Commission president Jacques Delors, who opted out of the presidential election two years ago, to be prime minister.
Lionel Jospin, who is leading the Socialist election campaign, gathered only 18 percent with Delors' daughter, ex-labour minister Martine Aubry, close behind at 16 percent.
Looking at a main campaign issue, surveys found an overwhelming majority of voters backing a sharp cut in working hours as part of a strategy to curb record unemployment.
BVA said 61 to 34 percent backed a Socialist plan to cut the working week to 35 hours from 39, with an even bigger majority saying wages should not be cut.
CSA found 68 to 26 percent backing a four-day week, with 67 to 31 percent saying they were prepared to take a five percent salary cut to compensate for the shorter working time.
